passages.happening:
‘Woe to the rebellious children,’ declares the LORD (verse 1), who carry out a plan that is not his and make an alliance against his will. ‘They set out to go down to Egypt without asking My advice, to seek shelter under Pharaoh’s protection’ (verse 2). But Pharaoh's protection will become their shame (verse 3). Their officials have reached Zoan and Hanes (verse 4), but Egypt will be useless to them (verse 5).

An oracle about the beasts of the Negev: through a land of hardship, of lions and vipers and flying serpents, they carry their wealth on donkeys and their treasures on camels to a people that cannot help (verse 6). ‘Egypt’s help is futile and empty; therefore I have called her Rahab Who Sits Still’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is the third woe of chapters 28 to 33, and the hidden plans of 29:15 come into the open. Judah's leaders are negotiating an alliance with Egypt against Assyria.

The setting is almost certainly the years leading to Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC. After Sargon II died in 705 BC, Hezekiah withheld tribute from Assyria, joined a coalition of rebel states and looked to Egypt for help. Egypt was then ruled by kings from Kush, eager to limit Assyria's power. Zoan was the royal city later called Tanis, in the northeastern delta. Hanes has not been securely identified; many place it at Heracleopolis in Middle Egypt.

The caravan of verse 6 carried Judah's treasure south through the dangerous desert of the Negev to pay for Egypt's help. Rahab was the name of a sea monster, a picture of chaos, and also a poetic name for Egypt. Isaiah calls Egypt the monster that sits still: big, fearsome and doing nothing.

Isaiah's warning proved true. When Sennacherib marched west in 701 BC, an Egyptian force met him at Eltekeh and was defeated, according to Sennacherib's own annals.
passages.later: The Assyrian field commander later taunted Jerusalem in the same words: ‘you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it’ (Isaiah 36:6). A psalm sings, ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God’ (Psalm 20:7).
passages.hard:
Was seeking an alliance with Egypt not simply prudent statecraft? Why does Isaiah treat it as sin?

From a political point of view, Hezekiah's advisers had good reasons. Assyria was brutal, Egypt was a major power with its own interest in resisting it, and small kingdoms routinely survived by making alliances. Isaiah's objection is not that diplomacy is wicked in itself. It is that the plan was made ‘without asking My advice’ (verse 2), that it rested Judah's safety on a foreign power rather than on the LORD, and that it went ahead in the face of a prophet's warning. Alliances in the ancient world were sealed with oaths before the gods of both sides, so a treaty with Egypt was also a statement of trust.

Events bore Isaiah out. Readers still disagree about how directly the chapter applies to modern politics, and these notes draw no line from it to any nation or policy of the present day. What it plainly teaches is that God's people are not to place in any human power the trust that belongs only to him.
passages.asks: Judah's leaders went to Egypt without asking God. Ask what plans you have made without asking him. And ask what you are carrying through the desert, at great cost, to buy help that cannot help.

passages.t: Prophesy pleasant things, and By repentance and rest
passages.happening:
‘Go now, write it on a tablet in their presence and inscribe it on a scroll’ (verse 8), a witness forever. They are rebellious people, children who will not listen to the LORD's instruction (verse 9). They tell the seers to stop seeing, and the prophets not to prophesy the truth: speak pleasant words, prophesy illusions, get out of the way, rid them of the Holy One of Israel (verses 10-11).

So the Holy One says their sin will be like a bulging high wall that collapses in an instant (verses 12-13), shattered like a potter's jar until no piece is big enough to scoop a coal from the fire (verse 14).

The Holy One of Israel had said, ‘By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence’ (verse 15). But they were not willing. They said they would flee on horses, and so they will flee; their pursuers will be faster (verse 16). A thousand will flee from one, until they are left like a pole on a mountaintop (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Isaiah is told to write his message down, so that later generations can see that the warning was given. The people do not want truth. They want pleasant words. They want the Holy One of Israel out of their way.

The bulging wall is a vivid picture: a wall with a crack that swells slowly and then collapses all at once. Sin that seems stable can fail in a moment.

Verse 15 is one of the great lines of the book. Salvation would have come through repentance and rest, strength through quietness and trust. The leaders chose horses instead. They would ride their horses only to flee.
passages.later: Paul warns of a time when people ‘with itching ears’ will gather teachers to suit their own desires (2 Timothy 4:3). And Jesus offers the rest Judah refused: ‘Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest’ (Matthew 11:28).
passages.asks: The people wanted prophets who would speak only pleasant things. Ask whether you prefer teachers who tell you what you want to hear. And ask what repentance and rest would look like in the place where you are reaching for horses.

passages.t: The LORD longs to be gracious
passages.happening:
‘Therefore the LORD longs to be gracious to you; therefore He rises to show you compassion, for the LORD is a just God’ (verse 18). Those who wait for him are happy.

People of Zion will weep no more. He will be gracious when they cry for help; when he hears, he will answer (verse 19). Though he gives them the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, their Teacher will no longer hide himself; they will see him with their own eyes (verse 20). Whether they turn to the right or the left, they will hear a voice behind them saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it’ (verse 21).

They will throw away their silver and gold idols as unclean things (verse 22). God will send rain on their seed, and the land will give rich food; cattle will graze in wide pastures (verses 23-24). Streams will flow on every hill (verse 25). The moon will shine like the sun and the sun seven times brighter, ‘on the day that the LORD binds up the brokenness of His people’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
After the woe comes grace. The same people who refused God's rest are told that God longs to be gracious to them. He waits to show compassion, as they should have waited for him.

The bread of adversity and the water of affliction are a picture of hard times. Even then, their Teacher would be near, and they would hear his voice telling them the way.

The idols are thrown away as unclean things, a sign of real repentance. Then the land is renewed and the light multiplied, on the day God binds up his people's wounds. The first hearers, whose land would be wounded by Assyria, were given a picture of its healing.
passages.later: A psalm promises, ‘I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go; I will give you counsel and watch over you’ (Psalm 32:8).
passages.asks: The LORD longs to be gracious and rises to show compassion. Ask whether you believe God longs for you in that way. And ask whether you are listening for the voice behind you that says, This is the way.

passages.t: Assyria shattered at the voice of the LORD
passages.happening:
‘Behold, the Name of the LORD comes from afar, with burning anger and dense smoke’ (verse 27). His breath is like a flood rising to the neck. He sifts the nations in a sieve of destruction and puts a bridle on the peoples (verse 28).

But his people will sing, as on the night of a holy festival, with hearts glad like those who walk to the sound of the flute up to the mountain of the LORD, the Rock of Israel (verse 29).

The LORD will make his majestic voice heard and his mighty arm seen, with consuming fire, cloudburst, storm and hail (verse 30). ‘For Assyria will be shattered at the voice of the LORD’ (verse 31). Every blow of the rod on Assyria will be met with tambourines and lyres (verse 32). Topheth has long been prepared; its pyre is deep and wide, and the breath of the LORD sets it ablaze like a stream of burning sulfur (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with a storm of judgment on Assyria and singing for Zion. The bridle in the jaws of the peoples pictures God leading the nations where he wills. And the joy promised his people is the joy of pilgrims going up to the mountain of the LORD to the sound of the flute.

Topheth was a place in the Valley of Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem, associated with child sacrifice. Here it becomes the pyre for Assyria's king. The place of Judah's worst sin becomes the place where the oppressor is judged.

The first hearers, facing the Assyrian army, were told that God's voice alone would shatter it.
passages.later: Josiah later ‘desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech’ (2 Kings 23:10). And Isaiah records the night the Assyrian army was struck (Isaiah 37:36).
passages.asks: God's people sing while the storm falls on their oppressor. Ask whether you can trust God with justice against those who have harmed you. And ask what it means that the place of worst sin became a place of judgment on the oppressor.
